accuracy.reason: Live Microsoft, Redis and AWS sources support cache-aside, staleness, eviction, local/shared failure and coalescing claims. Diagrams correctly depict hit/miss work and independent stale copy; no freshness/availability guarantee.

evidence.quote: Saving the price and removing the copy are separate steps. A reader can fetch $20 before the update, pause, then refill $20 after removal. The next cache hit still returns $20. Removal can also fail.
A product can be evicted before its TTL ends. Some configurations reject new entries when full instead of evicting existing ones.
Restarting one API process discards its local cache; other processes keep their copies. If the shared cache is unreachable, every API server using it loses access to those cached entries.

mechanisms.reason: Reader traces both read paths, late stale refill, expiration/eviction, local/shared visibility and duplicate source-work collapse. Failure responses actually bound database work.

evidence.quote: The entry is absent. The API reads the database, stores a copy in the cache, and returns the details.
Saving the price and removing the copy are separate steps. A reader can fetch $20 before the update, pause, then refill $20 after removal. The next cache hit still returns $20. Removal can also fail.
Many requests miss the same product together and repeat its database lookup. Coalescing requests lets concurrent readers share one in-progress lookup.

coherence.reason: One product/price example introduces reusable copy, application/key, updates, disappearance, placement and load before deciding. Declared concurrent-instance and commit prerequisites enable transfer without hidden infrastructure.

evidence.quote: In this example, the database owns the product record. Losing the cached copy must not lose the product.
The API checks and fills the cache explicitly. The cache does not fetch the product from the database on its own.
A seller changes the price from $20 to $25. The cached $20 is now stale.

decisions.reason: Checkout uses authority; descriptions may tolerate delay. Keys, shared/local choice, rejection under outage and when to avoid caching have explicit reasons and costs.

evidence.quote: A cache outage can turn most reads into database traffic. Limit fallback work to what the database can handle; reject excess requests or serve older data only where the product rules permit it.
For our product page, propose caching frequently read descriptions that tolerate a brief delay after edits. Keep checkout price validation tied to the order's authoritative data.
If requests rarely reuse results, or freshness is too hard to maintain, the cache may cost more than it saves.

clarity.reason: Short labelled definitions and concrete old/new prices keep all eight objectives understandable. Numerical learner transfers are supported; advanced limiter/coherence implementation is not silently assumed.

evidence.quote: Identifies the result to reuse. product:42 works for shared product details; prices in different currencies need distinct keys, such as product:42:USD.
Sets how long an entry may remain before it expires. A 60-second TTL does not refresh the product every minute; a later miss must load it again.

sourceChecks.claim: Microsoft caching guidance supports reuse benefits, initial source cost and copy-management tradeoffs.
Microsoft cache-aside shows application lookup, source fetch, fill and return; cached state can diverge.
Microsoft caching guidance supports result-specific keys and explicit application-managed copies; private sharing must preserve user distinctions.
Microsoft cache-aside disclaims consistency guarantees; the overlapping stale-refill trace is a valid counterexample.
Redis documents expiry and memory-pressure eviction, including noeviction rejection; neither is automatic source refresh.
AWS contrasts process-local and external caches with network, consistency and fleet-wide failure tradeoffs.
AWS explicitly recommends request coalescing and throttled dependency traffic to withstand empty/unavailable caches.
Microsoft says repeated costly reads favor caching; low reuse or correctness demands can outweigh its costs.
